name: Maximum in a Generic tree
html:
Welcome back, dear reader. So, how is it going? We hope you are enjoying this section on generic trees so far and learning a lot. So this problem is called MAXIMUM IN A GENERIC TREE.

Important Links : Problem Link, Question Video, Solution Video

Problem Discussion :

We are given a generic tree and we have to find the maximum value in that generic tree and return it. For instance:

In the above tree, the max is 60 so we will return 60 as our answer. We recommend you try to solve this problem on your own first and then move to the solution. You may refer to the question video if you have any doubts regarding the question.

Watch video Approach : High-Level Thinking:
  1. Expectation: Have a look at a generic tree shown below: Our expectation is that when we pass root as a parameter to the max function we should get the maximum value in this tree i.e. 120.
  2. Faith: Let us first try to think of this problem as a big problem. Now, let us try to find the small problem of the same kind because that is what we do in recursion, right? Have a look at the diagram shown below: A subtree of the given tree is highlighted in the diagram. So, the smaller problem would be to find the maximum in this tree. What do you think? Well, it is correct that the smaller problem would be to find the maximum element in a smaller-tree as compared to the given tree. But, which smaller tree should we find the max value for? Is it only the sub-tree highlighted above in the diagram or some other sub-tree? Have a look at the diagram shown below (fig-5)
  3. Relation: The root node of our tree has 3 children. So, we have 3 sub-trees from the root node. Now, according to our faith in recursion, we can find the max element in each of these sub-trees (as they are the smaller problems of the same kind). So, if we find out the max in the left subtree and the middle as well as in the right subtree (as shown in fig-5), we now have reduced the problem to a great extent. How? Think about it!!! By finding the max value in the left sub-tree, we have already compared all the elements in the left sub-tree i.e. 20, 50 and 60. Also, we have just made a recursive call here, we have not done anything by ourselves. It is just our faith in recursion which is doing all the work here. Don't worry if it sounds absurd. We will analyze the working of this in the low-level thinking. Now, we have also found the maximum value in the middle sub-tree i.e. we have already compared the values 30, 70, 80, 90, 110, 120. Also, we have found the max value for the right subtree i.e. we have already compared the values 40 and 100.
    So, we have now got three max values, each from a sub-tree of the root node. Now, what will be the max value in the tree? As we discussed, we have reduced the problem to a great extent now. We can simply compare these values and the root node (as it has not been compared yet) and the maximum value out of these will be the max in the generic tree.
    So, the max value is 120 (which we got from the middle sub-tree).
    So, the relation is simple. We have to apply our faith in recursion for all the children of the root node and then compare the root node with the max value obtained from its sub-trees.

You may refer to the solution video if you have any doubts about the high-level thinking procedure explained above. Now that we have the high-level thinking and we know what we have to do, let's write the code for the same.

Watch video import java.io.*; import java.util.*; public class Main { private static class Node { int data; ArrayList< Node> children = new ArrayList< >(); } public static void display(Node node) { String str = node.data + " -> "; for (Node child : node.children) { str += child.data + ", "; } str += "."; System.out.println(str); for (Node child : node.children) { display(child); } } public static Node construct(int[] arr) { Node root = null; Stack< Node> st = new Stack< >(); for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) { if (arr[i] == -1) { st.pop(); } else { Node t = new Node(); t.data = arr[i]; if (st.size() > 0) { st.peek().children.add(t); } else { root = t; } st.push(t); } } return root; } public static int size(Node node) { int s = 0; for (Node child : node.children) { s += size(child); } s += 1; return s; } public static int max(Node node) { int m = Integer.MIN_VALUE; for (Node child : node.children) { int cm = max(child); if(cm>m) { m=cm; } } if(node.data>m) { m=node.data; } return m; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)); int n = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine()); int[] arr = new int[n]; String[] values = br.readLine().split(" "); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { arr[i] = Integer.parseInt(values[i]); } Node root = construct(arr); int m = max(root); System.out.println(m); // display(root); } }
java; true";

Specially for you: In the above code we have initially set max equal to Integer.MIN_VALUE. This can be treated as minus infinity. Actually, minus infinity is the identity for finding the max value. Like in addition, 0 is the identity meaning we add any number to 0 we get the same number or in multiplication 1 is the identity i..e. we multiply any number with 1, we get the number itself. Similarly, we compare any number with minus infinity, the max value out of the two will be the number itself. So, can you think about what is the identity for finding the minimum value?

So dear reader, we hope that you understood the above high-level thinking procedure and also understood the code. Now, let us do the low level thinking and find out how the above code is giving us our desired result.

Low-Level Thinking:

Let us try to understand and analyze how our above code is working. For that, let us consider a generic tree shown below:

Now let us analyze the code and the condition of the stack and trace the Euler path simultaneously to understand what is happening. We recommend you keep the code by your side as it is important to understand which line of code causes what execution in the recursion.

We start with the root node (it gets pushed into the recursion stack). The first line of code executes and the max is set to minus infinity. (Have a look at fig-7). A white dot at the root node indicates that we have entered the loop and a call is made to the first child of the root node i.e. 20. So, the Euler path moves to 20 (as shown in fig-7).

Now, when the Euler path reaches the left part of node (20) then the first line of the function executes and the max value for 20 is also set to minus infinity. But, the loop will not execute for node (20) as there is no child node of this node. So, the next line executes which compares minus infinity with the data of the node. Since the data of the node is greater, the max for node (20) is 20 itself. (look at fig-8)

Also, 20 will wipe out from the stack as its code is completely executed. This is shown in fig-8

Note: We don't want you to get confused dear reader. The dots at the leaf nodes are drawn with an orange color. These dots indicate the lines of code or rather the parts of code. 2 orange dots indicate that the loop is not executed, only the part before and after it is executed whereas the white dots on the non-leaf nodes indicate the number of child nodes for which they have been called. There is only one white dot at 10 means the call has been made for only one of its child nodes till now. Remember this point throughout this article.

Again, 10 is at the top of the stack. Therefore, we are inside the loop for the root node. Since the root node called upon the node (20), the max value at the root node also changes from minus infinity to 20. Now, the Euler path reaches from the root node to the node (30).

When we are at the left of the node (30), we make max=minus infinity. Then, we enter the loop and a call is made to the first child node of the node (30). (see fig-10) .

Here again, we make max= minus infinity and then the loop will not execute as there is no child node for 50. So, we compare the data of the node i.e. 50 to minus infinity and since 50 is greater, the max value becomes 50 and 50 gets wiped out of the stack and the max value=50 is returned to the previous call to node (30) and its max value now changes from minus infinity to 50.(see fig-11)

Now, the Euler path will reach the left of the node (60) (indicated by the second white dot on node(30) in fig-12) and again the max value will be minus infinity. So, this value will be compared to the node data and 60 will win and the max value for node(60) call will be 60.

Now comes the interesting part. The loop is completed for node (30) as 60 will wipe out of the stack and both the children of node (30) have been traversed. Now, we are at the last line of code for node(30). Here, we compare the max value at node(30) to the max value we got from node(60). The max value at node(30) is already 50 (which we got from node(50)). So, 60 is greater than 50. Therefore, the max value at node(30) will be updated to 60 and since it is also completed, it will wipe out of the stack.

Now, only one node is left to traverse. Dear reader, we request you to traverse the Euler path on your own and find the final max value. The diagram below shows the final state of the tree and the stack after we complete the Euler path.

So, this is how our code is working and we are able to find the maximum value in this tree. Hope this procedure is clear to you. If you have any doubts regarding the above low-level thinking, you may refer to the solution video to understand this procedure more easily and clear all your doubts. Now let's move to the time and space complexity analysis:

Watch video Analysis: Time Complexity:

The time complexity of the above solution is O(n) as we are traversing all the nodes of the tree to find the maximum value.

Space Complexity:

Without Considering Recursion Space: Since we have not used any extra data structure therefore the space complexity of this solution is O(1).

Considering the Recursion Space: If we consider the recursion space then the stack has at most logn elements in it at a time (we will learn about this later in this section). So, the space complexity considering the recursion space will be O(logn).

Also, this is the best case and the average case space complexity. The worst case complexity will be O(n) if the tree is a skewed tree (if all the nodes are either on the left side or on the right side.) An example of left and right skewed trees is shown below:

Hope that you have understood everything. If you still have any doubts regarding anything in the procedure or in the code, you may refer to the complete solution video to clear all your doubts.

Watch video Suggestions:

Here are some suggestions from our side that you do not want to miss:

  1. The understanding of recursion is a must to understand trees in depth. We recommend you solve the questions in the recursion and backtracking section first and then come back if you are facing difficulties in understanding the recursion of the code.
  2. We recommend you solve this problem once again on your own and trace the Euler path and the condition of the stack simultaneously so that you can understand the concepts in depth and in a better way. Till then, Happy Coding!!!
